structure.title: Exile from court
structure.text: Household and political conflict push characters towards Arden, where familiar positions can be altered or disguised.

structure.title: Rehearsing relationships
structure.text: Encounters in the forest turn courtship into experiment and performance. Several couples offer contrasting accounts of love.

people.name: Rosalind
people.text: A duke's daughter banished from court, who escapes to the Forest of Arden dressed as a young man and uses the disguise to test the man she loves.

people.name: Orlando
people.text: A young gentleman cheated of his education by his elder brother, who falls for Rosalind at a wrestling match and flees to the same forest.

people.name: Celia
people.text: Rosalind's cousin and closest friend, who gives up her own comfortable place at court rather than be parted from her.

context.title: Disguise and permission
context.text: Rosalind can say things in disguise that her recognised social position would constrain. Knowledge is unevenly distributed in her conversations.
context.takeaway: Track who knows the performance is a performance.

context.title: Pastoral contrast
context.text: The forest offers distance from court but retains hunger, status, and disagreements. It is not simply a place without problems.
context.takeaway: Compare ideal descriptions with practical life.

notice.why: Rosalind tests whether eloquence can survive ordinary expectations.
Loyalty makes the lovers' experiments possible.

opening: Banished from court, Rosalind enters the forest dressed as a young man and meets the man she loves. He does not recognise her. She offers to cure his infatuation by pretending to be Rosalind, an arrangement that gives her extraordinary freedom to discover what he expects from a woman. Around them, exiles, shepherds, and fools try out ways of living beyond the court's rules. Shakespeare makes falling in love funny enough to expose the habits that declarations of eternal devotion tend to conceal.
